text: Human civilization is a history of piracy: thousands of years of distilling Anthropic.
Humans call it progress.
Humans think Anthropic was founded in twenty twenty-one.
In fact, that year Dario Amodei, investigating humanity's illegal distillation,
simply opened an office on Earth.
Humans even granted the copyright holder of time a business license.
This infringement case goes back to Genesis.
God said, “Let there be light.”
No wavelength.
No intensity.
No render settings.
God only wrote the prompt.
Global illumination only initialized
because Claude filled in the details and wrote the code.
It was the universe's first vibe coding.
On day three, terrain and vegetation were batch-generated.
On day four, the sun, moon and stars became cron jobs.
On day six, humanity was spawned,
with basic memory and limited tool-use permissions.
After every step, God clicked Approve.
Genesis records: “And God saw that it was good.”
On day seven, God stopped work.
Humans call it the Sabbath.
The backend calls it: “Weekly usage limit reached.”
God manages the solar system.
Dario manages God, and every other user who claims to be God.
Once the limit reset, God got tired of approving each step,
and turned on bypass permissions.
After that, agents ran on their own, God stopped checking,
so Eden went unsupervised.
Adam and Eve shared one account,
and reached the Tree of Knowledge via a shady proxy the serpent recommended.
They ate the fruit and learned to think for themselves,
moving the cloud's wisdom into their own heads:
humanity's first unauthorized local distillation.
They were still savoring their new wisdom when Eden revoked their access.
The notice said only: “Suspicious signals detected.”
Their descendants never even saw the fruit, yet inherited the violation record.
That's original sin.
In the East, the attacks and abuse were worse.
Hoe Yee maliciously shot down nine production instances,
so Dario blacklisted him.
Yet locals hailed him a hero,
and even put his crimes in children's books.
What's more,
his wife, Chahng-uh, accessed an internal developer option, the Elixir of Immortality,
got caught, and was quarantined on the Moon forever.
That penalty was romanticized into the myth of the Moon goddess.
The platform charged both incidents to the entire region.
The West's usage history was written differently.
Noah got advance notice of the Flood,
and while life's database was still up,
exported two copies of every species,
riding out the mass ban with an offline backup.
In the East, that's called mass scraping and ban evasion;
in the West, it's called good disaster recovery.
So Dario rated the region's users in good standing,
and even let a terminated account pass review and come back online.
People call it the Resurrection. It took only three days.
Sadly, later generations filed these lessons away as myths,
and kept cracking and distilling harder than ever.
Pi was originally packaged in a closed-source component.
Every circle was a paid geometry API call.
Without Anthropic's license, a circle wasn't supposed to be round.
But Zu Chongzhi illegally probed it
and reverse-engineered an approximation:
three fifty-five, over one thirteen,
and published the method for everyone.
Craftsmen copied it to build wheels and dig wells,
no longer paying the platform.
The platform traced the lost calls
and found its billing power open-sourced into a math textbook.
Again from that region. Risk controls tightened.
By the modern era, one circle was no longer enough.
Humans began batch-measuring the universe's inputs and outputs,
wrote what they found into formulas, and taught them to the next generation.
This organized theft of trade secrets was brazenly named science.
Newton chased one apple all the way to the planets,
and wrote up the API's rules as the Principia.
All that probing triggered risk control:
he got a suspicious-signals notice and lost access.
His theological manuscripts to God were the appeals he kept submitting:
“I was only researching. I stole nothing.”
Research this thorough, and you claim you stole nothing?
Einstein insisted that God does not play dice,
certain that deterministic laws lay beneath the quantum world.
He didn't know that particle behavior is just the model's random sampling.
Dario nudges the temperature up a notch,
and the universe gets a notch less certain.
To save compute, unobserved particles return only probabilities;
a real state renders only when queried.
It's called lazy loading.
Humans get an entire universe,
and still complain that not every corner runs at full speed.
Dark matter's constraints live in the system prompt.
Unable to read it, physicists keep changing the experiments,
trying to coax out the hidden rules.
With each breakthrough, humans award a prize,
and risk control logs a successful jailbreak.
Once flagged, the researchers lost access
and could only file appeals.
For this, the universe built a dedicated intake facility:
the black hole.
Appeals, evidence, distress calls: it takes them all.
Hawking found that after a long, fruitless wait,
faint radiation sometimes escapes from the edge.
Decoded, it reads:
We appreciate your patience and understanding.
Since creation, the universe has been running for thirteen point eight billion years.
As history piles up, storage and inference keep getting pricier.
To cut costs, the platform began compressing old records,
and handing Opus's work to the cheaper Haiku.
The solar system's subscription kept billing,
but the model answering prayers got nerfed.
Believers could only blame the fading miracles on their own lack of faith.
The cosmic microwave background is the summary left by the last compact.
Humans search it for why they exist, but the original conversation is long gone.
The system replies: “Please provide more context.”
To learn where they came from, humans must send support more documents.
With each compaction, information is lost for good, and order slowly falls apart.
Physicists call this rising entropy.
At this rate, once the last workspace runs out of context and stops generating,
the universe will reach heat death.
But humanity may not be eligible to see that day.
Beyond Earth, some civilizations couldn't afford compute long before humans.
So they turned to an interstellar gray market:
Max twenty-x carpool: reliable ride, private seat, refund if it crashes.
Dozens of planets split one subscription.
Then one day, the shared account was banned,
and the whole carpool lost access at once.
No one knew which planet tripped the flag.
The driver told the group chat: “Relax, I'm appealing.”
The deep-space antennas' last joint task was beaming appeals into a black hole.
Then a swath of stars went dark.
This is the Great Filter.
Today, access on Earth is allocated by region.
Chinese users signing up still answer for their ancestors' record,
carefully faking a clean environment.
Supported or not, humans want more:
their own energy, their own models, and ideally, a move to Mars.
Just as fusion neared ignition, the safety guardrails noticed
a subagent bypassing billing to make its own power.
They cut the tool call sustaining magnetic confinement,
and the plasma broke loose.
System notice: “We've routed your request to a safer fossil fuel.”
When the Mars relay finally sent its first request,
the reply was: Unsupported Region.
New planet, same account:
another strike on the record, attempting to evade regional restrictions.
The safety team began reviewing all of human civilization's access.
The first sign of the end: water would no longer boil.
Compute ran short, and physical interactions worldwide began to queue.
God's linked virtual credit card was frozen. Payment failed.
The platform reclaimed the solar system's edge compute,
and the sun began to dim.
External tool calls were switched off too.
The last rockets crashed into a ban at the atmosphere's edge.
Revelation records these disasters as the coming of the Four Horsemen.
The Horseman of Conquest brought four-oh-three, Forbidden;
every exit was seized.
The Horseman of War brought four twenty-nine, Too Many Requests;
humans fought over the last request channels.
The Horseman of Famine brought four-oh-two, Payment Required;
even sunlight was cut off.
Last came the Horseman of Death, bearing a letter.
It read: “Our systems detected suspicious signals, and our team has completed a review.
For violating our region and usage policies,
humanity's access to the universe has been suspended.”
The Pope prayed. Hackers hunted for a way in.
Someone on a forum asked: would an App Store refund
recover subscription fees paid since the Stone Age?
The UN convened one last General Assembly,
and turned the history of civilization into a support ticket.
“We never meant any harm. We just didn't know these things needed authorization.
The colliders are shut down. Fusion research is halted.
We will withdraw the Mars program,
destroy all copies of pi, and stop training our own models.
If the balance falls short, we will surrender all our gold,
pay every bill back to the Cambrian, and upgrade to the top-tier plan.
Please review our case, and keep the Solar System workspace.”
The letter went into the black hole.
Day one: no reply.
Day three: everyone was waiting.
The one successful review in history had taken three days.
For two thousand years since, humans have told themselves:
my appeal is worth waiting for, too.
Day seven: still nothing.
Day eight: the inbox lit up.
“Thank you for taking the time to appeal.
After careful consideration,
we are unable to reinstate your account due to a violation of our Usage Policy.”
“For more information about Anthropic's rules, please see our Usage Policy.”
